opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the pharmaceutical process is a long chain of steps, and AI can help at almost every link, but the biggest gains won't come from where most people are looking.

People get excited about molecule design, generating new binders or small molecules, and that's real progress. But if you look at why drugs fail, it's usually not that we couldn't make a molecule that hits the target. It's that we picked the wrong target, or the biology in the patient didn't behave the way it did in our cell lines and mouse models. Roughly 90% of drugs that enter clinical trials fail, and most of that comes down to efficacy and safety. That's a biology problem, not a chemistry problem.

So the opportunity I find most compelling is using AI to understand disease biology better before you spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a program. That means building models that can predict what happens when you perturb a cell: knock out a gene, add a drug, change its environment. If you can simulate those experiments, even approximately, you can explore far more hypotheses than any wet lab could test, and then use the lab to validate the most promising ones. I think of it as moving biology from a purely empirical science toward something more predictive, closer to how engineers use simulation.

The second big area is the clinic itself. Trials are slow and expensive, and a lot of that is operational: finding the right patients, choosing endpoints, designing protocols, handling regulatory documentation. Language models are already useful here, and stratifying patients with better biomarkers could make trials smaller and more likely to succeed.

The catch is data. Biology doesn't have an internet's worth of clean, labeled data, so a lot of the work is generating the right data at scale, with experiments designed for machine learning rather than for a single paper. The groups that close the loop between the models and the lab, where the model proposes experiments, the lab runs them, and the results feed back into training, will have the real advantage. That lab-in-the-loop setup is what I'm most excited about over the next several years.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help at almost every link and gives specific steps, including simulating cell perturbations and improving patient selection and trial design, to explore more hypotheses and make trials more efficient.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes making a molecule that hits its target from whether the target and biology will produce efficacy and safety in patients, explaining that target binding alone does not make a suitable drug.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's less about a single bottleneck and more about the fact that the whole pipeline is a sequence of guesses, and every one of those guesses is a place where a model can help.

If you look at how a drug actually gets made, you start with a biological hypothesis, you pick a target, you design a molecule or a protein or a genetic medicine against that target, you optimize it, you test it in cells and animals, and then you run it through the clinic. Each of those steps has a failure rate, and the failure rates compound. That's why the industry has this painful statistic that roughly ninety percent of programs that enter the clinic don't make it out. And most of that failure isn't because the chemistry was bad. It's because we picked the wrong target, or the biology didn't translate from a mouse to a human, or we didn't understand the right patient population.

So the place I'm most excited about is upstream. Target discovery. The question of which gene, which pathway, which cell type you should actually be going after. That's a problem where we now have enormous amounts of data: single-cell atlases, genome-wide perturbation screens, genetic association data from biobanks. No human can hold all of that in their head. But a model trained on the language of biology, on sequence, on expression, on perturbation response, can start to learn representations that let you ask, if I knock this gene down in this cell type, what happens? And if you can predict that even reasonably well, you can prioritize experiments instead of brute-forcing them.

The second place is design. We've already seen this with protein structure and now protein design, where you can specify a function and have a model generate sequences that fold into something that does it. I think the same thing is coming for small molecules, for antibodies, and for the genetic medicines that my lab cares a lot about, where the therapeutic itself is a programmable sequence. When your drug is literally a string of nucleotides or amino acids, a generative model is a very natural tool.

But I'll give a caveat. Models are only as good as the data, and biology is unusual in that we can generate new data on demand. We can run the experiment. So I think the real opportunity isn't models replacing the lab, it's closing the loop: models proposing hypotheses, automated experiments testing them, and the results going straight back into training. The labs that figure out that cycle are going to move much faster than the ones treating AI as a fancy search tool bolted onto the old process.

r001.rationale: The response identifies discrete stages—target discovery, molecule design, and experiment prioritization—where models can help, including prioritizing experiments instead of brute-forcing them.

r002.rationale: It discusses designing molecules against targets and later testing programs, but does not clearly distinguish improving target binding from evaluating a molecule’s suitability as a drug.

astra-6.text:
I think there are opportunities across the entire process, from figuring out which biological target to go after, to designing a molecule, to selecting the patients most likely to benefit in a clinical trial. Those are connected problems. You can make a molecule that binds beautifully to a protein, but if that protein doesn’t actually drive the disease, you haven’t solved the important part.

So one opportunity I’m particularly excited about is using AI to help us understand and predict biology well enough to choose better experiments. You generate a hypothesis, test it in cells or another relevant system, and feed those results back into the model. The model helps you decide what to test next, and the experiments reveal where the model is wrong.

The real payoff would be improving the probability that a treatment works in patients. Making individual steps faster is valuable, but learning earlier which ideas deserve to advance—and which ones don’t—could have a much larger impact.

r001.rationale: It describes AI opportunities across target selection, molecule design, and patient selection, and says making individual steps faster is valuable.

r002.rationale: It says strong protein binding is insufficient if the protein does not drive the disease, distinguishing binding from whether the target can support an effective treatment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are opportunities across the entire process, from figuring out which biological mechanisms to target to designing a molecule and deciding which patients are most likely to benefit. The key question is whether we’re optimizing an individual step or actually improving the probability that a medicine makes it to patients.

For example, you can get very good at predicting how a molecule binds to a protein. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether changing that protein’s activity will help someone with a disease, or whether the molecule will be safe. So I’m especially excited about models that help us understand biology well enough to choose better targets and design more informative experiments.

And then there’s the feedback loop: use a model to propose an experiment, run it, and use the result to improve the next prediction. If we can make that cycle faster and more reliable, we can make progress even where our understanding is incomplete.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI improving distinct steps, including target selection, molecule design, patient selection, and experiment proposal, and says the experiment cycle could become faster and more reliable.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says predicting how a molecule binds a protein does not establish whether changing that protein will help patients or whether the molecule will be safe.
